procedural_history.impugned_order: Final judgment and order dated 27.05.2014 passed by the High Court of Kerala at Ernakulum in Criminal M.C. No.2641 of 2007.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondent No.3 filed Criminal M.C. No.2641 of 2007 before the High Court of Kerala seeking to quash the final report filed in Crime Case No.5 of 2002. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the FIR, charge-sheet, and all consequent proceedings arising therefrom pending as C.C. No.2682 of 2002.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, aggrieved by the dismissal of his petition (Criminal M.C. No.1732/2004) and the order quashing the FIR/charge-sheet against respondent No.3, filed two SLPs (Special Leave Petitions), including the present SLP (Criminal Appeal No. 408 of 2018), in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court granted leave and allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order in Cri. M.C.No. 2641 of 2007.

directions: Impugned order passed in Criminal M.C No. 2641/2007 is set aside.
C.C. No.2682 of 2002 on the file of the JMFC-II, Ernakulum is restored to its file for being tried on merits in accordance with law.

If the Magistrate finds that the material brought on record against any person(s) including the appellant herein in the evidence indicating the involvement of any such person(s) in commission of the alleged offences, he will be free to proceed against any such person(s) in accordance with law and bring the proceedings to its logical end uninfluenced by any of our observations.

issue.issue_text: Whether a subsequent FIR, which is in the nature of a counter-complaint, is legally maintainable or is liable to be quashed.

facts: A trustee (Respondent No. 2) filed a first FIR against the appellant (Chief Executive Trustee), the treasurer (Respondent No. 3), and three bank officials, alleging they conspired to defraud the Trust.
Subsequently, the appellant filed a second FIR against the treasurer (Respondent No. 3), alleging fraud and forgery. This second FIR is considered a counter-complaint.
The High Court quashed the second FIR, reasoning that a person cannot face two trials on the same set of facts.
law: The Supreme Court clarified that while lodging two FIRs for the exact same incident by the same complainant is not permissible, this prohibition is restricted.
The law does not prohibit the filing of a counter-FIR by an accused from the first FIR, which alleges a different version of the same or a connected incident.
Such a subsequent FIR, when it is in the nature of a counter-complaint, is legally maintainable and can be tried on its merits.
application: The Court applied the law to the facts and found that the second FIR was legally maintainable for three main reasons:
1. **Different Complainants:** The second FIR was not filed by the same person who filed the first one; it was filed by the appellant, who was an accused in the first case.
2. **Nature of the Complaint:** The second FIR was a counter-complaint against one of the other parties involved (Respondent No. 3), presenting a rival version of events.
3. **Different Allegations and Parties:** The first FIR was against five people with one set of allegations, whereas the second FIR was based on different allegations against a single person.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the second FIR, being a counter-complaint filed by a different person with different allegations, was legally maintainable and should not have been quashed. The Court held that there is no legal prohibition against such a subsequent FIR and restored the case for trial on its merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the FIR/charge-sheet filed against respondent No.3, which was in the nature of a counter-complaint.

facts: A first FIR was filed by respondent No. 2 against the appellant, respondent No. 3, and three bank officials.
Subsequently, the appellant filed a second FIR, which was a counter-complaint, against respondent No. 3.
Respondent No. 3 approached the High Court to quash the second FIR, arguing that he could not be made to face two trials on the same set of facts.
The High Court allowed respondent No. 3's petition and quashed the second FIR/charge-sheet.
law: There is no legal prohibition against filing a second FIR if it is in the nature of a counter-complaint.
A second FIR filed as a counter-complaint is legally maintainable and can be tried on its merits.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court committed a jurisdictional error by quashing the second FIR without properly adverting to the law on counter-complaints.
The Court distinguished this case from situations where a second FIR is filed by the same person, noting that here it was a counter-complaint filed by a different party (the appellant).
It was also noted that the first FIR was against five individuals with one set of allegations, whereas the second FIR contained different allegations specifically against respondent No. 3.
The Court reasoned that since the second FIR was a legally maintainable counter-complaint, it should be allowed to proceed to trial on its merits.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in quashing the FIR/charge-sheet. It held that the second FIR, being a counter-complaint filed by a different person with distinct allegations, was legally maintainable and should be tried on its merits. Therefore, the High Court's order was set aside.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a subsequent FIR, which is in the nature of a counter-complaint, is legally maintainable or is liable to be quashed.
appellant_arguments: The subsequent FIR, being a counter-complaint, was legally maintainable and the Magistrate was justified in directing the police to register and investigate it.
The registration of the counter-complaint is not barred by Section 161 or 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
respondent_arguments: The subsequent FIR and the resulting charge-sheet are liable to be quashed because a person cannot be made to face two trials on the same set of facts and for the same offences in two different courts.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the FIR/charge-sheet filed against respondent No.3, which was in the nature of a counter-complaint.
appellant_arguments: The High Court erred in quashing the FIR/charge-sheet because the counter-complaint was legally maintainable and should be tried on its merits.
respondent_arguments: The High Court was justified in quashing the FIR/charge-sheet to prevent the respondent from having to face two trials based on the same set of facts.

cases.case_name: Upkar Singh v. Ved Prakash & Ors.
cases.principle: For the proposition of law laid down after examining previous case laws on the subject.

cases.case_name: Surender Kaushik & Ors. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.principle: For reiterating the aforesaid principle laid down in Upkar Singh v. Ved Prakash & Ors.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The law on the subject which governs the controversy is settled by the decision of the Court in Upkar Singh vs. Ved Prakash & Ors., (2004) 13 SCC 292.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court committed a jurisdictional error in quashing the subsequent FIR/charge-sheet filed by the appellant because it failed to advert to the established law on the subject. A subsequent FIR that is in the nature of a counter-complaint is legally maintainable and is entitled to be tried on its merits.
legal_tests_applied: The legal principle that a subsequent FIR, when it is in the nature of a counter-complaint, is legally maintainable and should not be quashed on the grounds of being a second FIR.
policy_considerations: Criminal cases, including those arising from counter-complaints, should be tried and decided on their merits based on the evidence adduced by the parties to bring the proceedings to a logical end.
